content:
The frenulum is the band of tissue on the underside of the penis that connects the foreskin to the glans (head of the penis).

Normally, the frenulum has enough length and flexibility to allow the foreskin to move backwards comfortably when the penis is erect. If it is too short, tight or scarred, it can pull on the underside of the glans and restrict normal movement.

At Beverley Clinic in North-West London, we provide frenuloplasty to release a tight or short frenulum. Frenuloplasty can be performed on its own when the foreskin is otherwise normal, or frenulum treatment can be performed together with circumcision when both the frenulum and foreskin are contributing to the problem.

You can usually see it most clearly when the foreskin is pulled backwards.

The frenulum helps connect and control the movement of the foreskin. It is also a sensitive area containing nerves and blood vessels.

A normal frenulum should allow the foreskin to retract comfortably without excessive tension or significant pulling on the glans.

What is a short frenulum or frenulum breve?

Frenulum breve simply means that the frenulum is shorter than required for comfortable movement.

When the penis is soft, a short frenulum may cause little or no problem.

The tightness often becomes much more obvious during an erection because the penis lengthens and the foreskin moves backwards.

If the frenulum cannot comfortably accommodate this movement, it becomes tense and can pull on the underside of the glans.

Some patients have always had a short frenulum. Others develop tightness following repeated tearing, inflammation or scarring.

What are the symptoms of a tight frenulum?

Symptoms can include:

  • Tightness underneath the glans
  • A pulling or tugging sensation during an erection
  • Pain during sexual intercourse
  • Pain during masturbation
  • Tearing or splitting of the frenulum
  • Bleeding
  • Recurrent soreness underneath the glans
  • Difficulty comfortably retracting the foreskin during an erection
  • Downward pulling or bending of the glans
  • Anxiety about the frenulum tearing during sex

Some patients have only one of these symptoms, while others experience several.

Why does a tight frenulum cause pain during an erection?

As the penis becomes erect, the foreskin and penile skin need to move freely.

If the frenulum is too short, it reaches the limit of its movement before the rest of the skin does.

The frenulum then becomes tight and places tension on the underside of the glans.

This can produce a pulling or painful sensation, particularly when the foreskin is pulled backwards during sexual activity.

In more pronounced cases, the tension can visibly pull the glans downwards.

Can a tight frenulum cause the head of the penis to bend downwards?

Yes.

A significantly short frenulum can act like a tether underneath the glans.

During an erection, this tension can pull the glans downwards when the foreskin retracts.

The amount of pulling varies between patients.

If the downward movement disappears when the foreskin is moved forwards and the frenulum is no longer under tension, this can be a useful indication that the frenulum is contributing to the problem.

We assess this during examination.

Why does my frenulum keep tearing?

A short frenulum can be repeatedly stretched beyond its comfortable length during erections, masturbation or intercourse.

This can cause a small tear.

The tear may heal, but the resulting scar tissue can sometimes be less flexible than the original tissue.

The next time the frenulum is placed under tension, it may tear again.

Some patients therefore develop a cycle of:

  • tight frenulum
  • stretching during sex
  • tearing or bleeding
  • healing and scarring
  • further tightness

If this repeatedly occurs, surgical release of the tight tissue can provide a more definitive solution.

Why can a torn frenulum bleed so much?

The frenulum contains blood vessels.

A tear can therefore sometimes produce more bleeding than a patient expects from what appears to be a relatively small cut.

This can understandably be alarming.

Bleeding from a small tear will often stop with appropriate direct pressure, but persistent or heavy bleeding requires medical assessment.

With a tight frenulum, the restriction is primarily underneath the glans. The foreskin itself may be capable of retracting, but the frenulum becomes tense and prevents comfortable movement.

With phimosis, the opening of the foreskin itself is too tight to retract comfortably over the glans.

Some patients have both.

This distinction matters because the treatment is different.

If the foreskin itself retracts normally and the problem is isolated to the frenulum, frenuloplasty can treat the frenulum while preserving the foreskin.

If there is significant foreskin tightness or scarring as well, circumcision may need to be considered together with treatment of the frenulum.

Learn more about phimosis and tight foreskin →

How can I tell whether the problem is my frenulum?

Patients often describe being able to retract the foreskin when the penis is soft but experiencing tightness or pulling underneath the glans during an erection.

You may notice that:

  • The foreskin opening itself does not feel particularly tight
  • Tension is concentrated underneath the glans
  • The frenulum becomes visibly stretched
  • The glans is pulled downwards as the foreskin retracts
  • The same area repeatedly tears or bleeds
  • Moving the foreskin forwards relieves the tension

An examination is the best way to determine whether the problem is the frenulum, foreskin or both.

What is frenuloplasty?

A frenuloplasty is a minor surgical procedure used to release and lengthen a short or tight penile frenulum.

The aim is to reduce the tension underneath the glans so that the foreskin and penile skin can move more comfortably.

The tight frenular tissue is carefully released and the area is allowed to heal in a way that provides greater length and movement.

The exact technique depends on the patient's anatomy and the appearance of the frenulum.

What happens during frenuloplasty at Beverley Clinic?

Before the procedure, we examine the penis to confirm that the frenulum is responsible for the symptoms and assess whether the foreskin itself is also tight or scarred.

For suitable patients, the procedure is performed under local anaesthetic, meaning that the area is numbed while you remain awake.

The tight frenulum is released to remove the restrictive band underneath the glans.

Depending on the anatomy and the wound, dissolvable stitches, medical skin glue, a combination of the two, or occasionally neither may be used.

We check that the frenulum has been adequately released before completing the procedure.

You receive detailed aftercare instructions before leaving the clinic.

If the problem is isolated to the frenulum, frenuloplasty can be performed without removing the foreskin.

This means that the foreskin remains present following the procedure.

This is an important distinction between frenuloplasty and circumcision.

Frenuloplasty: treats the tight frenulum while retaining the foreskin.

Circumcision: removes the foreskin.

Which procedure is appropriate depends on where the actual problem is located.

Frenuloplasty or circumcision?

This is one of the most important questions we assess.

If you have a normal foreskin with an isolated short frenulum, frenuloplasty may be all that is required.

If you have a short frenulum together with significant phimosis, foreskin scarring, recurrent foreskin problems or BXO / lichen sclerosis, treating the frenulum alone will not remove the underlying foreskin problem.

In those circumstances, circumcision with treatment of the frenulum may be more appropriate.

We therefore examine both the frenulum and foreskin rather than assuming that every patient with pulling underneath the penis requires the same procedure.

Learn more about adult circumcision →

Learn more about phimosis →

Learn more about BXO / lichen sclerosis →

Can the frenulum be treated during circumcision?

Yes.

If a patient requires circumcision and also has a tight, short or scarred frenulum, the frenulum can be assessed and treated as part of the circumcision procedure where appropriate.

This can be important cosmetically as well as functionally.

Leaving a significantly tight frenulum untreated can continue to produce pulling underneath the glans even though the foreskin has been removed.

We therefore assess the frenulum as part of our examination when circumcising patients with medical foreskin problems.

Can I have frenuloplasty if I am already circumcised?

Yes.

A patient can still have a tight or problematic frenulum after circumcision.

If the remaining frenular tissue is causing pulling, pain, recurrent tearing or an unsatisfactory appearance, we can assess whether further frenulum release is appropriate.

If there are also concerns about the amount or distribution of remaining foreskin or shaft skin, we assess these separately.

Learn more about re-circumcision and circumcision revision →

What if the frenulum has already torn?

A frenulum can occasionally tear sufficiently that the tightness improves afterwards.

However, this is not always the case.

The tear may heal with scar tissue, leaving the frenulum still tight or even less flexible than before.

Repeated tears can also produce an irregular or scarred appearance.

If you have had previous frenulum tears, we examine how the area has healed and whether there is persistent tension before deciding how it should be treated.

What if I have scar tissue around the frenulum?

Scar tissue can alter the flexibility of the frenulum.

It may develop after repeated tearing, inflammation, injury or previous surgery.

If there is significant scarring, we assess whether it is confined to the frenulum or whether the surrounding foreskin is also affected.

A white or extensively scarred foreskin can indicate a separate foreskin condition such as BXO / lichen sclerosis, which changes how the problem should be approached.

BXO / lichen sclerosis →

The area underneath the glans can initially feel sensitive and the wound will change in appearance as it heals.

If dissolvable stitches are used, these gradually loosen as healing progresses.

You will receive instructions explaining how to look after the area and when to contact us.

The final result should not be judged from the appearance during the first few days because swelling and wound healing temporarily change the appearance of the frenulum.

When can I return to work?

This depends on your occupation and how you feel after the procedure.

Many patients with desk-based work require relatively little time away, whereas jobs involving strenuous physical activity may require longer.

We provide individual advice following your procedure.

When can I exercise after frenuloplasty?

Strenuous activity that causes significant friction, stretching or pressure around the wound should be avoided during the early healing period.

Return to exercise gradually according to your healing and the instructions provided after your procedure.

When can I have sex after frenuloplasty?

The frenulum is placed under considerable tension during erections, masturbation and sexual intercourse.

It is therefore important to allow the wound to heal sufficiently before placing it under this tension.

At Beverley Clinic, we generally advise avoiding sexual intercourse and masturbation for at least two weeks and until the wound is sufficiently healed.

If the wound remains tender, open or incompletely healed at two weeks, you should wait longer.

Follow the individual advice provided after your procedure.

What are the risks of frenuloplasty?

Frenuloplasty is a surgical procedure and complications can occur.

Potential risks include:

  • Bleeding
  • Infection
  • Swelling
  • Bruising
  • Pain or tenderness
  • Wound separation
  • Scarring
  • Altered sensation
  • Cosmetic dissatisfaction
  • Persistent tightness or pulling
  • Need for further treatment

The frenulum is a sensitive area, so changes in sensation can occur following surgery.

We discuss the relevant risks with you before treatment.

The location of the tension is important.

When examining a patient, we look at how easily the foreskin opening passes over the glans and what happens to the frenulum as the foreskin moves backwards.

If the foreskin itself moves freely but the frenulum becomes tight and pulls the underside of the glans, the frenulum may be the main problem.

We also look for previous tears, scar tissue and downward pulling of the glans.

If the foreskin is also tight or scarred, we assess that separately rather than expecting frenuloplasty to correct a foreskin problem.

This allows us to decide whether the patient needs frenuloplasty alone or circumcision with treatment of the frenulum.
